title: The opening sequence for every task
summary: The same short routine runs before each task starts.

steps.n: At the start the candidate sets the k alias, completion and a dry run variable in the shell.
The task names a cluster context, a namespace and an exact end state.
The candidate pastes the context command from the task and checks the current context.
If a field is unfamiliar the candidate searches the allowed docs by object name and copies an example.
The candidate applies the smallest change that meets the requirement.
A get and describe confirm exactly what the task asked for before moving on.

title: Imperative command to finished YAML
summary: Generate, edit one block, apply and check.

steps.n: The candidate runs a create command with dry run and output as YAML into a file.
kubectl writes a complete manifest with sensible defaults and the right apiVersion.
The candidate adds only the missing part, such as a volume mount or a toleration.
kubectl apply sends the manifest to the API server.
The API server validates and stores the object and the controller creates pods.
A get and describe confirm that the pods are running with the new setting.

title: Upgrading a control plane then a worker
summary: One minor version at a time in the documented order.

steps.n: The admin upgrades kubeadm on the control plane and runs plan to see available versions.
kubeadm apply upgrades the static pod manifests to the new version.
The admin drains the control plane node, upgrades kubelet and kubectl, restarts and uncordons it.
On a worker the admin drains the node so its pods move elsewhere.
kubeadm upgrade node updates the local config and the kubelet package is upgraded and restarted.
The admin uncordons the worker and checks that all nodes are Ready at the new version.

title: From a certificate request to a working user
summary: A user is created with a certificate, a role and a kubeconfig.

steps.n: The user creates a private key and a certificate signing request for the name jane.
The admin creates a CSR object and approves it, and the API server signs the certificate.
The admin creates a role that allows get and list on pods in one namespace.
A role binding connects the role to the user jane in that namespace.
Set-credentials and set-context add the certificate and a context for the user.
Auth can-i confirms a pod listing is allowed and a pod deletion is denied.

title: Why a pod is Pending
summary: The scheduler checks each node against the pod requirements.

steps.n: A pod with a node selector and no toleration is created and has no node yet.
Node A has a taint the pod does not tolerate, so it is rejected.
Node B does not carry the label in the selector, so it is rejected as well.
The scheduler records FailedScheduling with the exact reason for each node.
The candidate describes the pod and reads that one taint and one label are the blockers.
Adding the missing label to a node lets the scheduler place the pod there.

title: Following a request to a pod
summary: A name is resolved and traffic reaches an endpoint.

steps.n: The client asks CoreDNS for the service name in its namespace.
CoreDNS returns the cluster IP of the service.
The client sends a request to the cluster IP and port.
The service rules pick a ready pod address from the endpoint list.
Traffic is sent to the chosen backend pod on its container port.
If the endpoint list is empty the candidate checks that the selector matches the pod labels.

title: A claim binds to a volume
summary: Class, mode and size decide binding.

steps.n: A claim asks for 5Gi, ReadWriteOnce, with the class named fast.
The class uses WaitForFirstConsumer, so the claim waits and shows Pending.
A pod that mounts the claim is created and the scheduler picks a node.
The scheduler tells the provisioner which zone the volume must be in.
The provisioner creates a volume of the right size and mode in that zone.
The claim binds to the volume and the pod can mount it and start.

title: A top down troubleshooting walk
summary: Symptom first, then one layer down at a time.

steps.n: The candidate writes down exactly what fails and for whom.
Describe and events are read for scheduling, image and probe messages.
Container logs, including the previous container, are read for errors.
Node conditions and the kubelet service state are checked for a stopped service.
Static pod manifests and logs of the API server, scheduler and controller manager are checked.
Only one change is made at a time and the original symptom is checked again.

title: A benchmark fix cycle
summary: Run, fix one control, run again.

steps.n: The admin runs kube-bench and gets a list of failed checks.
One check says the kubelet accepts anonymous requests.
The admin copies the kubelet config file before changing it.
Anonymous access is set to false and authorization mode is set to Webhook.
The kubelet restarts and applies the new settings to node requests.
The check now passes and an anonymous request returns unauthorised.

title: Gate an image before it runs
summary: Scan, pin and admit only what passes.

steps.n: The build pushes an image to the internal registry with a digest.
Trivy scans the image and reports vulnerabilities by severity.
High severity findings are fixed and the image is rebuilt.
The manifest refers to the image by its digest so the content cannot change under a tag.
An admission policy checks the registry prefix and that a digest is present.
A pod from an allowed registry is created and a lookalike image name is rejected.

title: Failure and recovery: the empty snapshot
summary: A backup that was never verified fails the restore.

steps.n: The candidate runs a snapshot command with no certificate flags.
The command waits and times out, leaving a zero byte file.
The error scrolled away and the candidate goes on to the next task.
A later task asks for a restore and the command fails on the empty file.
Listing the file shows zero bytes and the problem is clear.
The candidate takes the endpoint and certificate paths from the etcd static pod manifest.
Snapshot save with endpoints, cacert, cert and key flags produces a real file.
Snapshot status shows a hash and revision, and the restore then succeeds into a new directory.

title: Failure and recovery: the API server that did not return
summary: Audit flags without volume mounts stop the control plane.

steps.n: The admin copies the API server manifest to a safe place before editing.
The admin adds the audit policy and log path flags to the command section.
The kubelet sees the changed manifest and recreates the API server pod.
The new pod has no mount for the policy file, so the process exits at start.
kubectl commands time out because the API server is not running.
The admin reads the logs with the container runtime tool and finds file not found for the policy.
The manifest gets a volume and mount for the policy file and the log directory.
The kubelet recreates the pod, the API server starts and audit events begin to appear in the log file.
